etymologies.etymologyHTML: Abbreviation of chatter. The bird sense refers to the sound of its call.

definitions.definition: To be engaged in informal conversation.
To talk more than a few words.

quote.text: We would get totally stoned and usually drunk too and chat a load of nonsense into the small hours.

definitions.definition: (informal, slang, often as chatting) To chat shit (to speak nonsense, to lie).
(by extension, Philippines) To send a text message via Facebook Messenger instead of via SMS.
To exchange text or voice messages in real time through a computer network, as if having a face-to-face conversation.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, “Foreword”, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: Reg liked a chat about old times and we used to go and have a chinwag in the pub.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) An exchange of text or voice messages in real time through a computer network, resembling a face-to-face conversation.
(metonymically, originally video games) The entirety of users, viewed collectively, in a chat room, especially the chat room accompanying a live stream.

quote.citation: 2024 September 11, Fatima Payman, 00:48 from the start, in Skibidi Senator Payman + 100,000 aura‎[1] (video), archived from the original on September 12, 2024:
quote.text: Chat, is this prime minister serious?

definitions.definition: (by extension, nonstandard, humorous) Familiar term of address for users on social media other than a chat room, as in "guys."
(Internet, uncountable, with or without "the") A chat room, especially (in later use) one accompanying a videoconference or live stream.

quote.citation: 1997, Meg Booker, The Insider's Guide to America Online, page 256:
quote.text: While there are chats for various interest groups (games, Internet, sports), you can also  […]

definitions.definition: (countable) Any of various small Old World passerine birds in the muscicapid tribe Saxicolini or subfamily Saxicolinae that feed on insects.
(countable) Any of several small Australian honeyeaters in the genus Epthianura.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Compare chit (“small piece of paper”), and chad.

definitions.definition: A small potato, such as is given to swine.

quote.citation: 1978, Joan Thirsk, Edith Holt Whetham, H. P. R. Finberg, The Agrarian History of England and Wales: Volume 8, 1914-1939, Cambridge University Press, →ISBN, page 5:
quote.text: Wheat and potatoes were traditionally cash crops, though they also provided tail corn for the poultry and chats for the pigs

definitions.definition: (mining, local use) Mining waste from lead and zinc mines.

quote.citation: 2006, Thomas Pynchon, Against the Day, Vintage, published 2007, page 441:
quote.text: Frank had been looking at calcite crystals for a while now [...] among the chats or zinc tailings of the Lake County mines, down here in the silver lodes of the Vita Madre and so forth.

definitions.definition: (British, Australia, New Zealand, World War I military slang) A louse (small, parasitic insect).

quote.citation: 1977, Mary Emily Pearce, Apple Tree Lean Down, page 520:
quote.text:
'Do officers have chats, then, the same as us?'
'Not the same, no. The chats they got is bigger and better, with pips on their shoulders and Sam Browne belts.'

quote.citation: 2007, How Can I Sleep when the Seagull Calls?, →ISBN, page 18:
quote.text: May a thousand chats from Belgium crawl under their fingers as they write.

quote.citation: 2013, Graham Seal, The Soldiers' Press: Trench Journals in the First World War, →ISBN, page 149:
quote.text: Trench foot was a nasty and potentially fatal foot disease commonly caused by these conditions, in which chats or body lice were the bane of all.
